newsitem.title: USA: Tropical Storm Hortense not strengthening.
newsitem.headline: Tropical Storm Hortense not strengthening.

text.p: Hurricane warnings remained posted for the British and U.S. Virgin Islands on Sunday, but may be downgraded as Tropical Storm Hortense was not strengthening, the National Hurricane Centre said.
Tropical storm warnings were still in effect for the north-eastern Caribbean islands from Martinique to Saint Maarten, and a tropical storm watch for Puerto Rico.

But forecasters said that by 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT) Hortense's maximum sustained winds had decreased to 55 mph (89 kph) from 60 mph (95 kph) three hours earlier. It was still moving west-northwest at 10 mph (16 kph).
Hortense's centre was located 155 miles (250 km) south-east of St. Croix in the U.S. Virgins, at latitude 16.2 north and longitude 63.0 west, having passed over the French Island of Guadeloupe.
"Hurricane warnings remain in effect for the British and U.S. Virgin islands but may be downgraded to tropical storm warnings if Hortense does not strengthen," said the National Hurricane Centre.
"There is no significant strengthening expected and maximum sustained winds have decreased."

A hurricane or tropical storm warning indicates that hurricane or tropical storm conditions are expected within 24 hours. Hurricane and tropical storm watches are posted 36 hours ahead of possible landfall.
Hortense requires sustained winds of 74 mph (119 kph) to become a hurricane
Hortense initially gathered strength in the wake of Hurricane Fran, which hit the U.S. coast on Thursday, wreaking havoc through the Carolinas and killing at least 22 people.
Hortense was upgraded to tropical storm status at mid-morning on Saturday.

The string of tiny Leeward Islands -- including Martinique, Dominica, Guadeloupe, Antigua, Montserrat, the U.S. Virgin Islands and the British Virgin Islands -- immediately issued tropical storm warnings and urged residents to prepare.
Forecasters said it was too early to predict whether Hortense, which was dumping rain of up to 10 inches (25 cm) along its path, would threaten the U.S. mainland.
